{{Short description|Theorem in algebra mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], more specifically [[abstract algebra]] and [[commutative algebra]], '''Nakayama's lemma''' &mdash; also known as the '''Krull–Azumaya theorem'''<ref name="Nagata">{{harvnb|Nagata|1975|loc=§A.2}}</ref> &mdash; governs the interaction between the [[Jacobson radical]] of a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] (typically a [[commutative ring]]) and its [[finitely-generated module|finitely generated]] [[Module (mathematics)|modules]].  Informally, the [[lemma (mathematics)|lemma]] immediately gives a precise sense in which finitely generated modules over a commutative ring behave like [[vector space]]s over a [[field (mathematics)|field]]. It is an important tool in [[algebraic geometry]], because it allows local data on [[algebraic variety|algebraic varieties]], in the form of modules over [[local ring]]s, to be studied pointwise as vector spaces over the [[residue field]] of the ring.

The lemma is named after the Japanese mathematician [[Tadashi Nakayama (mathematician)|Tadashi Nakayama]] and introduced in its present form in {{harvtxt|Nakayama|1951}}, although it was first discovered in the special case of [[ideal (ring theory)|ideals]] in a commutative ring by [[Wolfgang Krull]] and then in general by [[Goro Azumaya]] ([[#CITEREFAzumaya1951|1951]]).<ref>{{harvnb|Nagata|1975|loc=§A.2}}; {{harvnb|Matsumura|1989|p=8}}</ref><ref>According to Matsumura (1970), Nakayama was said to have disliked the name "Nakayama's lemma".</ref> In the commutative case, the lemma is a simple consequence of a generalized form of the [[Cayley–Hamilton theorem]], an observation made in classic texts by Zariski–Samuel (1958) and Atiyah–Macdonald (1969).<ref>Zariski–Samuel, §IV.7, Lemma 2 (alternative proof) and Atiyah–Macdonald, Ch. 2, Corollary 2.5</ref>  The special case of the [[noncommutative algebra|noncommutative]] version of the lemma for right ideals appears in [[Nathan Jacobson]] ([[#CITEREFJacobson1945|1945]]), and so the noncommutative Nakayama lemma is sometimes known as the '''Jacobson–Azumaya theorem'''.<ref name="Nagata" /> The latter has various applications in the theory of [[Jacobson radical]]s.<ref>{{harvnb|Isaacs|1993|loc=Corollary 13.13, p. 184}}</ref>

==Statement==
Let <math>R</math> be a [[commutative ring]] with identity 1.  The following is Nakayama's lemma, as stated in {{harvtxt|Matsumura|1989}}:

'''Statement 1''':  Let <math>I</math> be an [[Ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] in <math>R,</math> and <math>M</math> a [[finitely generated module]] over <math>R.</math>  If <math>IM=M,</math> then there exists <math>r \in R</math> with <math>r \equiv 1\; (\operatorname{mod} I)</math> such that <math>rM = 0.</math>

This is proven [[#Proof|below]].   A useful mnemonic for Nakayama's lemma is "<math>IM = M \implies im = m</math>".  This summarizes the following alternative formulation:

'''Statement 2''':  Let <math>I</math> be an [[Ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] in <math>R,</math> and <math>M</math> a [[finitely generated module]] over <math>R.</math>  If <math>IM=M,</math> then there exists an <math>i \in I</math> such that <math>im = m</math> for all <math>m \in M.</math>
:''Proof'': Take <math>i = 1 - r</math> in Statement 1.

The following corollary is also known as Nakayama's lemma, and it is in this form that it most often appears.<ref>{{harvnb|Eisenbud|1995|loc=Corollary 4.8}}; {{harvtxt|Atiyah|Macdonald|1969|loc=Proposition 2.6}}</ref>

'''Statement 3''': If <math>M</math> is a finitely generated module over <math>R,</math> <math>\mathrm{J}(R)</math> is the [[Jacobson radical]] of <math>R,</math> and <math>\mathrm{J}(R)M=M,</math> then <math>M = 0.</math>
:''Proof'': <math>1 - r</math> (with <math>r</math> as in Statement 1) is in the Jacobson radical so <math>r</math> is invertible. Thus <math>M = (r^{-1})(rM)=0.</math><ref>There is also a simple direct proof of Nakayama's lemma in this form.  ''Proof:'' Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that <math>x_1,...,x_n</math> generate ''M'', with <math>n\geq 1</math> being the smallest number with this property.  Since <math>x_n \in \mathrm{J}(R)M,</math> there are <math>a_i\in\mathrm{J}(R)</math> with <math display="inline">x_n= \sum_{i=1}^n a_ix_i,</math> or <math display="inline">(1-a_n)x_n=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} a_ix_i.</math>  (Here, the set of generators <math>\{x_1,...x_{n-1}\}</math> is regarded as empty and the sum equal to 0 if <math>n=1.</math>) Because <math>a_n\in\mathrm{J}(R),</math> <math>1-a_n</math> is a unit [if not, <math>1-a_n</math> is in some maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak{m},</math> but then <math>a_n\in\mathfrak{m}</math> as <math>\mathfrak{m}\supset\mathrm{J}(R),</math> so <math>1= (1-a_n)+a_n\in\mathfrak{m},</math> contradiction], and so <math display="inline">x_n=(1-a_n)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}a_ix_i.</math>  Therefore, <math>x_1,...,x_{n-1}</math> generate ''M''.  This contradicts the minimality of ''n'', and so <math>M=0,</math> Q.E.D.</ref>

More generally, one has that <math>\mathrm{J}(R)M</math> is a [[Essential extension|superfluous submodule]] of <math>M</math> when <math>M</math> is finitely generated.

'''Statement 4''': If <math>M</math> is a finitely generated module over <math>R,</math> <math>N</math> is a submodule of <math>M,</math> and <math>M = N + \mathrm{J}(R)M,</math> then <math>M = N.</math>
:''Proof'': Apply Statement 3 to <math>M/N.</math>

The following result manifests Nakayama's lemma in terms of generators.<ref>{{harvnb|Eisenbud|1995|loc=Corollary 4.8(b)}}</ref>

'''Statement 5''': If <math>M</math> is a finitely generated module over <math>R</math> and the images of elements <math>m_1,\cdots,m_n</math> of <math>M</math> in <math>M/\mathrm{J}(R)M</math> generate <math>M/\mathrm{J}(R)M</math> as an <math>R/\mathrm{J}(R)</math>-module, then <math>m_1,\cdots,m_n</math> also generate <math>M</math> as an <math>R</math>-module.
:''Proof'': Apply Statement 4 to <math>\textstyle{N=\sum_{i} Rm_i}.</math>

If one assumes instead that <math>R</math> is [[completion (ring theory)|complete]] and <math>M</math> is separated with respect to the <math>I</math>-adic topology for an ideal <math>I</math> in <math>R</math>, this last statement holds with <math>I</math> in place of <math>\mathrm{J}(R)</math> and without assuming in advance that <math>M</math> is finitely generated.<ref>{{harvnb|Eisenbud|1995|loc=Exercise 7.2}}</ref>  Here separatedness means that the <math>I</math>-adic topology satisfies the [[T1 space|''T''<sub>1</sub>]] [[separation axiom]], and is equivalent to <math>\textstyle{\bigcap_{k=1}^\infty I^k M = 0.}</math>

==Consequences==

===Local rings===
In the special case of a finitely generated module <math>M</math> over a [[local ring]] <math>R</math> with [[maximal ideal]] <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>, the quotient <math>M/\mathfrak{m}M</math> is a vector space over the field <math>R/\mathfrak{m}</math>.  Statement 5 then implies that a [[basis of a vector space|basis]] of <math>M/\mathfrak{m}M</math> lifts to a minimal set of generators of <math>M</math>. Conversely, every minimal set of generators of <math>M</math> is obtained in this way, and any two such sets of generators are related by an [[invertible matrix]] with entries in the ring.

==== Geometric interpretation ====
In this form, Nakayama's lemma takes on concrete geometrical significance. Local rings arise in geometry as the [[germ (mathematics)|germ]]s of functions at a point. Finitely generated modules over local rings arise quite often as germs of [[section (fiber bundle)|sections]] of [[vector bundle]]s. Working at the level of germs rather than points, the notion of a finite-dimensional vector bundle gives way to that of a [[coherent sheaf]]. Informally, Nakayama's lemma says that one can still regard a coherent sheaf as coming from a vector bundle in some sense. More precisely, let <math>\mathcal{M}</math> be a coherent sheaf of <math>\mathcal{O}_X</math>-modules over an arbitrary [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] <math>X</math>. The [[stalk (mathematics)|stalk]] of <math>\mathcal{M}</math> at a point <math>p\in X</math>, denoted by ''<math>\mathcal{M}_p</math>'', is a module over the local ring <math>(\mathcal{O}_{X,p},{\displaystyle {\mathfrak {m}}_{p}})</math> and the fiber of <math>\mathcal{M}</math> at <math>p</math> is the vector space <math>\mathcal{M}(p) = \mathcal{M}_p/\mathfrak{m}_p\mathcal{M}_p</math>. Nakayama's lemma implies that a basis of the fiber <math>\mathcal{M}(p)</math> lifts to a minimal set of generators of ''<math>\mathcal{M}_p</math>''. That is:
* Any basis of the fiber of a coherent sheaf ''<math>\mathcal{M}</math>'' at a point comes from a minimal basis of local sections.
Reformulating this geometrically, if <math>\mathcal{M}</math> is a locally free <math>\mathcal{O}_X</math>-module representing a vector bundle <math>E \to X</math>, and if we take a basis of the vector bundle at a point in the scheme <math>X</math>, this basis can be lifted to a basis of sections of the vector bundle in some neighborhood of the point. We can organize this data diagrammatically<blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
E|_p & \to & E|_U & \to & E \\
\downarrow & & \downarrow & & \downarrow \\
p & \to & U & \to & X
\end{matrix}</math></blockquote>where <math>E|_p</math> is an n-dimensional vector space, to say a basis in <math>E|_p</math> (which is a basis of sections of the bundle <math>E_p \to p</math>) can be lifted to a basis of sections <math>E|_U \to U</math> for some neighborhood <math>U</math> of <math>p</math>.

===Going up and going down===
{{main|Going up and going down}}
The '''going up theorem''' is essentially a corollary of Nakayama's lemma.<ref>{{harvnb|Eisenbud|1995|loc=§4.4}}</ref>  It asserts:

* Let <math>R \hookrightarrow S</math> be an [[integral extension]] of commutative rings, and <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> a [[prime ideal]] of <math>R</math>. Then there is a prime ideal <math>\mathfrak{q}</math> in <math>S</math> such that <math>\mathfrak{q}\cap R = \mathfrak{p}</math>.  Moreover, <math>\mathfrak{q}</math> can be chosen to contain any prime <math>\mathfrak{q}_1</math> of <math>S</math> such that <math>\mathfrak{q}_1\cap R \subset \mathfrak{p}</math>.

===Module epimorphisms===
Nakayama's lemma makes precise one sense in which finitely generated modules over a commutative ring are like vector spaces over a field. The following consequence of Nakayama's lemma gives another way in which this is true:

*If <math>M</math> is a finitely generated <math>R</math>-module and <math>f:M\to M</math> is a surjective endomorphism, then <math>f</math> is an isomorphism.<ref>{{harvnb|Matsumura|1989|loc=Theorem 2.4}}</ref>

Over a local ring, one can say more about module epimorphisms:<ref name="Griffiths">{{harvnb|Griffiths|Harris|1994|p=681}}</ref>

*Suppose that <math>R</math> is a local ring with maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>, and <math>M,N</math> are finitely generated <math>R</math>-modules. If <math>\phi:M\to N</math> is an ''<math>R</math>''-linear map such that the quotient <math>\phi_\mathfrak{m}:M/\mathfrak{m}M \to N/\mathfrak{m}N</math> is surjective, then <math>\phi</math> is surjective.

===Homological versions===
Nakayama's lemma also has several versions in [[homological algebra]].  The above statement about epimorphisms can be used to show:<ref name="Griffiths" />

* Let <math>M</math> be a finitely generated module over a local ring. Then <math>M</math> is [[projective module|projective]] if and only if it is [[free module|free]]. This can be used to compute the [[Grothendieck group]] of any local ring <math>R</math> as <math>K(R) = \mathbb{Z}</math>.
A geometrical and global counterpart to this is the [[Serre–Swan theorem]], relating projective modules and coherent sheaves.

More generally, one has<ref>{{harvnb|Eisenbud|1995|loc=Corollary 19.5}}</ref>
* Let <math>R</math> be a local ring and <math>M</math> a finitely generated module over ''<math>R</math>''. Then the [[projective dimension]] of <math>M</math> over <math>R</math> is equal to the length of every minimal [[free resolution]] of <math>M</math>. Moreover, the projective dimension is equal to the [[global dimension]] of <math>M</math>, which is by definition the smallest [[integer]] <math>i \geq 0</math> such that
::<math>\operatorname{Tor}_{i+1}^R(k,M) = 0.</math>
:Here <math>k</math> is the residue field of ''<math>R</math>'' and <math>\text{Tor}</math> is the [[tor functor]].

=== Inverse function theorem ===
Nakayama's lemma is used to prove a version of the [[inverse function theorem]] in algebraic geometry:

* Let <math display="inline">f: X \to Y</math> be a [[projective morphism]] between [[quasi-projective varieties]]. Then <math display="inline">f</math> is an isomorphism if and only if it is a [[bijection]] and the [[Zariski tangent space|differential]] <math display="inline">df_p</math> is injective for all <math>p \in X</math>.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McKernan |first=James |author-link=James McKernan |title=The Inverse Function Theorem |url=https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~jmckerna/Teaching/13-14/Spring/203C/l_5.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220909204021/https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~jmckerna/Teaching/13-14/Spring/203C/l_5.pdf |archive-date=2022-09-09}}</ref>

==Proof==
A standard proof of Nakayama's lemma (Statement 1) uses the following technique popularized by {{harvtxt|Atiyah|Macdonald|1969}}.<ref>{{harvnb|Matsumura|1989|p=7}}: "A standard technique applicable to finite ''A''-modules is the 'determinant trick'..."  See also the proof contained in {{harvtxt|Eisenbud|1995|loc=§4.1}}.  The same technique was used earlier in the proofs of two lemmata in Zarski–Samuel (1958, §IV.7 and §V.1) ''Commutative Algebra I'' (pp. 216, 255).</ref>  We first prove the following assertion:<ref>[[Nakayama's lemma#CITEREFEisenbud1995|Eisenbud 1995]], Theorem 4.3</ref>
* Let ''M'' be an ''R''-module generated by ''n'' elements, and let <math>\varphi\colon M\to M</math> be an [[Module homomorphism|''R''-linear map]].  If there is an ideal ''I'' of ''R'' such that <math>\varphi(M)\subseteq IM,</math> then there is a [[monic polynomial]] <math>p(t) = t^n + p_1t^{n-1} +\cdots + p_n</math> with <math>p_k\in I^k,</math> such that <math>p(\varphi)=0</math> as an endomorphism of ''M''.
This assertion is precisely a generalized version of the [[Cayley–Hamilton theorem]], and the proof proceeds along the same lines.  

''Proof of assertion:'' On the generators <math>x_i</math> of ''M'', one has a relation of the form
:<math>\varphi(x_i) = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j</math>
where <math>a_{ij}\in I</math>.  Thus
:<math>\sum_{j=1}^n\left(\varphi\delta_{ij} - a_{ij}\right)x_j = 0,</math>
where <math>\delta_{ij}</math> in the [[Kronecker delta]], and we are now regarding ''M'' as an <math>R[\varphi]</math>-module with <math>\varphi x_i=\varphi(x_i).</math>  The required result follows by multiplying by the [[Adjugate matrix|adjugate]] of the matrix <math>[\varphi\delta_{ij}-a_{ij}]</math> and invoking [[Cramer's rule]].  One finds then that <math>\det(\varphi\delta_{ij}-a_{ij})=0</math>, so the polynomial
:<math>p(t) = \det(t\delta_{ij}-a_{ij})</math>

has the required properties.  This proves the assertion.  

To complete the proof of Nakayama's lemma, assume that <math>IM=M</math> and take <math>\varphi</math> to be the identity on ''M''.  Then define polynomial ''p'' as above.  Then
:<math>r=p(1) = 1+p_1+p_2+\cdots+p_n</math>
has the required properties, <math>r \equiv 1\; (\operatorname{mod} I)</math> and <math>rM = 0</math>. 

==Noncommutative case==
A version of the lemma holds for right modules over [[non-commutative ring|non-commutative]] [[unital ring]]s ''R''.  The resulting theorem is sometimes known as the '''Jacobson–Azumaya theorem'''.<ref>{{harvnb|Nagata|1975|loc=§A2}}</ref>

Let J(''R'') be the [[Jacobson radical]] of ''R''. If ''U'' is a right module over a ring, ''R'', and ''I'' is a right ideal in ''R'', then define ''U'''''·'''''I'' to be the set of all (finite) sums of elements of the form ''u'''''·'''''i'', where '''·''' is simply the action of ''R'' on ''U''. Necessarily, ''U'''''·'''''I'' is a submodule of ''U''.

If ''V'' is a [[maximal submodule]] of ''U'', then ''U''/''V'' is [[Simple module|simple]].  So ''U'''''·'''J(''R'') is necessarily a subset of ''V'', by the definition of J(''R'') and the fact that ''U''/''V'' is simple.<ref>{{harvnb|Isaacs|1993|p= 182}}</ref> Thus, if ''U'' contains at least one (proper) maximal submodule, ''U'''''·'''J(''R'') is a proper submodule of ''U''. However, this need not hold for arbitrary modules ''U'' over ''R'', for ''U'' need not contain any maximal submodules.<ref>{{harvnb|Isaacs|1993|p=183}}</ref> Naturally, if ''U'' is a [[Noetherian ring|Noetherian]] module, this holds. If ''R'' is Noetherian, and ''U'' is [[Finitely generated module|finitely generated]], then ''U'' is a [[Noetherian module]] over ''R'', and the conclusion is satisfied.<ref>{{harvnb|Isaacs|1993|loc=Theorem 12.19, p. 172}}</ref> Somewhat remarkable is that the weaker assumption, namely that ''U'' is finitely generated as an ''R''-module (and no finiteness assumption on ''R''), is sufficient to guarantee the conclusion. This is essentially the statement of Nakayama's lemma.<ref name="Isaacs">{{harvnb|Isaacs|1993|loc=Theorem 13.11, p. 183}}</ref>

Precisely, one has:
:'''Nakayama's lemma''': Let ''U'' be a [[Finitely generated module|finitely generated]] right module over a (unital) ring ''R''.  If ''U'' is a non-zero module, then ''U'''''·'''J(''R'') is a proper submodule of ''U''.<ref name="Isaacs" />

===Proof===
Let <math>X</math> be a finite subset of <math>U</math>, minimal with respect to the property that it generates <math>U</math>. Since <math>U</math> is non-zero, this set <math>X</math> is nonempty. Denote every element of <math>X</math> by <math>x_i</math> for <math>i\in \{1,\ldots,n\}</math>. Since <math>X</math> generates <math>U</math>,<math>\sum_{i=1}^n x_i R = U</math>.

Suppose <math>U\cdot \operatorname J(R) = U</math>, to obtain a contradiction. Then every element <math>u \in U</math> can be expressed as a finite combination <math>u=\sum\limits_{s=1}^{m}u_{s}j_{s}</math> for some <math>m\in\mathbb{N},\, u_s\in U,\, j_s \in \operatorname J(R), \,s=1,\dots,m</math>.

Each <math>u_s</math> can be further decomposed as <math>u_s = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} x_i r_{i,s}</math> for some <math>r_{i,s}\in R</math>. Therefore, we have

<math>u=\sum_{s=1}^{m}\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i r_{i,s} \right)j_s = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}x_i \left(\sum_{s=1}^{m}r_{i,s}j_s\right)</math>.

Since <math>\operatorname J(R)</math> is a (two-sided) ideal in <math>R</math>, we have <math>\sum_{s=1}^{m}r_{i,s}j_s \in \operatorname J(R)</math> for every <math>i\in\{1,\dots,n\}</math>, and thus this becomes

:<math>u= \sum_{i=1}^n x_i k_i</math> for some <math>k_i\in \operatorname J(R)</math>, <math>i=1,\dots,n</math>.

Putting <math>u=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i</math> and applying distributivity, we obtain

:<math>\sum_{i=1}^n x_i (1 - k_i) = 0</math>.

Choose some <math>j\in\{1,\dots,n\}</math>. If the right ideal <math>(1-k_j) R</math> were proper, then it would be contained in a maximal right ideal <math>M\neq R</math> and both <math>1-k_j</math> and <math>k_j</math> would belong to <math>M</math>, leading to a contradiction (note that <math>\operatorname J(R)\subseteq M</math> by the definition of the Jacobson radical). Thus <math>(1-k_j)R=R</math> and <math>1-k_j</math> has a right inverse <math>(1-k_j)^{-1}</math> in <math>R</math>. We have

:<math>\sum_{i=1}^n x_i (1 - k_i) (1 - k_j)^{-1} = 0</math>.

Therefore,

:<math>\sum_{i\neq j} x_i (1 - k_i) (1 - k_j)^{-1} = -x_j</math>.

Thus <math>x_j</math> is a [[linear combination]] of the elements from <math>X\setminus\{x_j\}</math>. This contradicts the minimality of <math>X</math> and establishes the result.<ref>{{harvnb|Isaacs|1993|loc=Theorem 13.11, p. 183}}; {{harvnb|Isaacs|1993|loc=Corollary 13.12, p. 183}}</ref>

==Graded version==

There is also a graded version of Nakayama's lemma. Let ''R'' be a ring that is [[graded ring|graded]] by the ordered monoid of non-negative integers, and let <math>R_+</math> denote the ideal generated by positively graded elements. Then if ''M'' is a graded module over ''R'' for which <math>M_i = 0</math> for ''i'' sufficiently negative (in particular, if ''M'' is finitely generated and ''R'' does not contain elements of negative degree) such that <math>R_+M = M</math>, then <math>M = 0</math>. Of particular importance is the case that ''R'' is a [[polynomial ring]] with the standard grading, and ''M'' is a finitely generated module.

The proof is much easier than in the ungraded case: taking ''i'' to be the least integer such that <math>M_i \ne 0</math>, we see that <math>M_i</math> does not appear in <math>R_+M</math>, so either <math>M \ne R_+M</math>, or such an ''i'' does not exist, i.e., <math>M = 0</math>.
